deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler builds tables of very large primes (up to about 4·10^6) using numbers of the form a^2+1. The previous page sets up a sieve. For each a ≤ 2000, attach every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) with p < a and a ≡ ±r_p (mod p), where r_p^2 ≡ −1 (mod p). Also attach 2 when a is odd. The result is the list of all prime divisors of a^2+1 that are smaller than a.

Coroll. 1: if no divisor is attached to a, then a^2+1 is prime. Reason: a composite N = a^2+1 has a prime factor p ≤ √N < a+1, so p ≤ a. Also p ≠ a, since a does not divide a^2+1. So p < a, and p would have been attached.

Coroll. 2: with a ≤ 2000 the table lists every prime of the form a^2+1 up to 4,000,000. So it yields certified primes above 10^5 and even above 10^6.

Coroll. 3: if exactly one divisor α < a is attached, then (a^2+1)/α is prime. Reason: the cofactor has no prime factor below a, and any composite cofactor would be at least (a+1)^2 > a^2+1. In particular, odd a with only 2 attached gives primes (a^2+1)/2. This produces every prime of the form (a^2+1)/2 up to about 2·10^6.

The argument is a sieve of Eratosthenes adapted to the polynomial x^2+1. It uses the root pairs ±r_p modulo p together with the size bound √(a^2+1) < a+1.
errors: Coroll. 3 as stated on this page is only valid if α divides a^2+1 to the first power. If α^2 | a^2+1, the cofactor (a^2+1)/α is divisible by α and is not prime. Euler corrects this himself in Scholion 1 on the next page: attach the highest power of α. The case α=2 is harmless because a^2+1 is never divisible by 4.
Minor: the limit 2,000,000 for (a^2+1)/2 is approximate. With odd a ≤ 1999 the actual maximum is (1999^2+1)/2 = 1,998,001.

ideas.what: Sieve over the values of a quadratic polynomial: for each prime p ≡ 1 mod 4, mark the residues a ≡ ±r_p (mod p); unmarked a give a^2+1 prime
ideas.modern_name: Polynomial sieve of Eratosthenes for n^2+1 (Landau's fourth problem context)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (this paper, E283) is commonly cited for the earliest such tables of primes n^2+1
ideas.where_published: E283, Novi Commentarii 9 (1764); also Euler's earlier remarks on a^2+1 divisors in his work on sums of two squares

ideas.what: Bound: a composite a^2+1 has a prime factor less than a, so sieving with primes < a suffices
If a^2+1 has exactly one (simple) prime factor below a, the cofactor is prime. This gives primes of the forms (a^2+1)/2, /5, /13, etc.
ideas.modern_name: Recognising cofactors as prime via the sieve limit; implicitly n^2+1 = p·q (a P2-type statement)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler for the tables; the almost-prime theory of n^2+1 is due to Iwaniec (1978)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, well-known sieve that Euler describes in a paper frequently cited for its tables of primes n^2+1. The multiplicity gap is fixed by Euler on the following page. Nothing here is uncredited or unexploited.
transcription_corrections: 'ſoles binarius' is printed as such but is presumably a typo for 'ſolus binarius'.
'relinquentur' in the print should probably read 'relinquuntur'/'relinquantur' (minor).
